name: PCB Trace Resistance
seoTitle: PCB Trace Resistance — Free Online Calculator
seoDesc: PCB Trace Resistance: work out ambient temperature from the trace width and the length. A free other calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the PCB Trace Resistance calculator the trace width, the length, the trace thickness and the resistivity and it returns ambient temperature. That makes it useful for whatever you happen to be working on. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the PCB Trace Resistance calculator work?
sections.html:
The PCB Trace Resistance calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports ambient temperature in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the trace width (W), the length (L), the trace thickness (T) and the resistivity (ρ).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the PCB Trace Resistance calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Ambient temperature=25 − 1 ÷ resistivity temperature coefficient (α) + resistance × trace thickness (T) × trace width (W) ÷ (resistivity temperature coefficient (α) × length (L) × resistivity (ρ))
Voltage drop=current × resistance

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Resistivity (ρ) = 0 cm, Resistivity temperature coefficient (α) = 0.0039 °C, Resistance = 10 Ω and Current = 10 A. Working through the relationship above gives Voltage drop = 100 V.

The point of the example is the scale, not the particular digits: swap in your own figures and the same relationship produces your answer.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Voltage drop = 100 V should be roughly the size you expected from Resistivity (ρ) = 0 cm and Resistivity temperature coefficient (α) = 0.0039 °C.

  • Shown in volts, and convertible to any of the 6 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Length, opening in centimeters
  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Resistance – ohms, opening in ohms
  • Electric current – ampere, opening in amperes

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The PCB Trace Resistance calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the trace width, the length and the trace thickness — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the PCB Trace Resistance calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns ambient temperature, derived from the trace width, the length and the trace thickness. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the PCB Trace Resistance calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the trace width, the length, the trace thickness and the resistivity, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter trace width (W) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Trace width (W) opens in millimeters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Voltage drop = 100 V. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the PCB Trace Resistance calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
